newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso gets green light for re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso gets green light for re-election.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso may run for an unprecedented second term next year after the Senate voted overwhelmingly on Wednesday to end a century-old ban on re-election.

Sixty-two of the Senate's 81 members voted in favour of a bill that allows presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second, consecutive term, 13 more than the three-fifths majority the legislation needed as a constitutional amendment. Fourteen senators voted against the bill and two abstained.

The bill, considered Cardoso's biggest political challenge since he took office in January 1995, officially became law shortly after the Senate vote when a joint session of Congress' two houses ratified it.

Brazil banned re-election when the republic was founded in 1889 to prevent a return to the authoritarian ways of its former Portuguese rulers. But Cardoso has argued that his programme to reform the economy and streamline the state was too big to complete in just one four-year term.
"What we re doing here is setting the foundations for continued economic stability and growth," said Jose Serra, a member of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB) before the vote.
Cardoso, who is considered favourite to win the October 1998 presidential race, had little comment on the vote. "The president was satisfied," a spokesman for the president said.

Analysts said Cardoso probably had more pressing worries. Reforms of the pension and civil service, considered crucial to the long-term stability of the government's economic plan, have been stuck for months in Congress.

In an attempt to reverse what, with the exception of the re-election bill, has been a dismal few months in Congress, Cardoso named influential deputy Luis Eduardo Magalhaes as his new chief whip in the fractious, multi-party lower house.

Magalhaes secured the approval of several government reforms while president of the Chamber of Deputies between 1995 and earlier this year. His power is enhanced by the clout of his father Sen. Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, a powerful political boss.

"People think Luis Eduardo will work magic but that's far from clear," said political analyst Ricardo Pedreira. "The real problem for Cardoso is that a lot of members of Congress are too conservative to accept the kind of reforms he wants."
